news-starship-booster-catch-2025.s: On 6 March 2025, in Texas, a huge Super Heavy booster rocket was caught in mid-air, not with a net, but with the arms of a tower. First the rocket lifted a spaceship up, then it separated and headed back down to the ground. It flew tail first, and its engines slowed it down gently. Two steel arms of the tower, called “chopsticks”, grabbed the rocket by special bits sticking out, and it stopped still in the air. A landing like this means the rocket is not thrown away, but can be refuelled and launched again. That day it worked for the third time in history.
a: With the arms of the tower

news-blue-ghost-moon.s: On 2 March 2025, the American lander “Blue Ghost” touched down gently on the Moon. It was built by a private company, not by a government. It landed in the Sea of Crises, which is not water but a dark, rocky plain. The lander stood straight on all four legs and did not fall over. Inside were ten NASA instruments. They measured how the Moon’s soil heats up and tried to collect dust. The lander could work for one Moon day, which is about 14 Earth days, while the Sun shines on it.

news-kolossalny-kalmar-2025.s: In March 2025, scientists filmed a live colossal squid in its natural sea for the first time. It happened in the Atlantic Ocean, near the South Sandwich Islands. A robot on a long cable went down six hundred metres and saw a see-through baby about thirty centimetres long. A grown-up colossal squid is the heaviest animal on Earth without a backbone, and its eyes are the biggest of any animal. Before, people had only seen squid that had been caught or found, but now they saw a live one!
a: A see-through baby, about thirty centimetres

news-thutmose-ii-tomb.s: In February 2025, Egypt announced that the tomb of the pharaoh Thutmose the Second had been found. He ruled about three and a half thousand years ago. The tomb is hidden in the mountains not far from the city of Luxor. Its entrance was found back in 2022, and people thought a pharaoh’s wife was buried there. But on pieces of broken jars made of white stone called alabaster, they read the name of Thutmose the Second. Two of the pieces also have the name of his wife, Hatshepsut, who later became a pharaoh herself. The tomb itself is almost empty: its things were moved to another place long, long ago.
a: The writing on pieces of broken jars

news-parker-closest-sun.s: On 24 December 2024, the space probe Parker flew closer to the Sun than any craft before it. It passed about six million kilometres from the Sun’s surface. That is very close: if the Sun were a ball, the probe was five steps away from it. The probe’s speed is a record: about 690 thousand kilometres an hour. A thick shield made of a special light material protects it from the heat, and behind the shield it is cool. After the flyby, the probe sent a signal to Earth that everything was fine. Scientists want to find out why the air around the Sun is so hot.

news-samyj-bolshoj-korall-2024.s: In November 2024, scientists told the world about the biggest coral in the world. It was found near the Solomon Islands in the Pacific Ocean. It is bigger than a blue whale and can even be seen from space. It is not one little animal, but almost a billion tiny polyps, relatives of jellyfish, which live together as one. It is about three hundred years old. It was found by accident: from above, it looked like an old sunken ship. The coral is brown, with bright spots on it, yellow, pink and blue.

job-pozharny.s: Hi! My name is Oliver and I'm a firefighter. My shift lasts a whole day and night, and in the morning the first thing I do is check the fire engine. I look to see if there is enough water, if the siren works, and if the ladder and the hoses are in place. A fire hose is a long pipe made of strong cloth: when water runs through it, it goes hard like a metal pipe. Then we train to be nimble and quick, and we visit schools to tell children how to stay safe from fire. At school, PE and science helped me most. Remember: in Russia, grown-ups call 101 for firefighters. In the UK it is 999, or 112. I love it when the day is calm and we all laugh together at lunch.
a: It goes hard, like a pipe
It goes soft, like a pillow

job-pediatr.s: Hi! My name is Emily and I'm a children's doctor, or in science words, a paediatrician. In the morning I put on my white coat and wait for babies and schoolchildren, together with their mums and dads. First we say hello and chat a little, so nobody is scared. Then I listen to how a baby breathes and how their heart beats, look at their throat and measure how tall they are. For this I have a stethoscope, a wooden spatula and a height chart. At school, biology and English helped me most: a doctor has to explain things very clearly. Did you know that a child's heart beats faster than a grown-up's? If a child is laughing at the end of the appointment, the day was a success.

job-medsestra.s: Hi! My name is Grace and I'm a nurse. My shift at the hospital starts with a round of the wards: I say hello to everyone and ask how they are. I measure temperatures and blood pressure and write the numbers down, so the doctor knows everything. My helpers are a thermometer, a blood pressure cuff and bandages. If someone feels sad, I can sit beside them and talk. At school, biology, maths and tidy handwriting helped me most. International Nurses' Day is on 12 May, the birthday of Florence Nightingale, a woman who showed how important good care for the sick is. In the evening I feel that the day was well spent.

job-feldsher.s: Hi! My name is Jack and I'm a paramedic. We drive an ambulance with flashing lights and a siren, so we can reach someone who needs help quickly. In the morning my team and I check that everything is in our big bag and in the ambulance. It holds a blood pressure cuff, a stethoscope, bandages and little boxes of medicine. When a call comes in, other drivers make way for us. I try to speak calmly and kindly, so the person doesn't worry. At school, biology and chemistry helped me most. In Russia, an ambulance is called on 103, and from a mobile also on 112. In the UK it is 999, or 112. The nicest thing is hearing “thank you”.

job-hirurg.s: Hi! My name is Charlotte and I'm a surgeon. A surgeon heals not only with knowledge but with her hands: for example, she helps when a broken bone needs to be mended carefully. In the morning I visit my patients, and then I get ready for an operation. I wash my hands for a long time, very carefully, and put on a cap, a mask and a clean gown. During the operation the person is fast asleep and feels nothing, and a whole team works beside me. A bright lamp, fine instruments, and a needle and thread help me. At school, biology, art and design and technology helped me most: you need nimble fingers. Surgeons practise tying tiny knots on special practice models.

job-stomatolog.s: Hi! My name is Harry and I'm a dentist, a doctor who looks after teeth. In the morning I switch on the bright lamp and get my room ready. Little children come to see me, and so do grandmas and grandads. I look at teeth with a little mirror, clean them, and show you the right way to hold a toothbrush. My helpers are a little mirror, a lamp and a soft little brush. I know how to tell jokes, so that children aren't scared. At school, biology, chemistry and clay modelling helped me most: teeth have to be made with care. Did you know that enamel on teeth is the hardest part of the whole human body? Grown-ups have 32 teeth, and little children have 20 baby teeth.

job-veterinar.s: Hi! My name is Sophie and I'm a vet, a doctor for animals. In the morning cats, dogs, hamsters and even parrots come to the clinic. First I talk to the owner, then I gently check the pet. I listen to the heart with a stethoscope, weigh the animal on the scales and look into its ears. Animals need to feel calm, so I speak in a quiet voice. At school, biology and science helped me most. Did you know that a cat has 18 toes: five on each front paw and four on each back paw? And I'm happy when a dog that has got better wags its tail.

job-farmacevt.s: Hi! My name is George and I'm a pharmacist, or, as people used to say, a chemist. In the morning I open the pharmacy and put boxes of medicine and vitamins on the shelves. When someone comes in, I read the doctor's prescription and find the right medicine. I always check the name carefully and explain how to take it. The scales, the computer and a big reference book help me. At school, chemistry, maths and paying close attention helped me most. The word “pharmacy” comes from Greek, and long ago it meant a “storehouse”. When a customer leaves with a smile, I know I have helped.

job-psiholog.s: Hi! My name is Hannah and I'm a psychologist. I help people understand their feelings: when they are scared, hurt or sad. In the morning I get my room ready and put out soft toys, paints and a box of building blocks. Children and grown-ups come to see me. We play, draw and talk, and I listen very carefully. A drawing sometimes helps to say what is hard to say in words. At school, biology, English and literature helped me most. The word “psychology” comes from Greek: “psyche” means “soul” and “logos” means “study”. After work I like to go for a walk and listen to the birds.

job-logoped.s: Hi! My name is Ella and I'm a speech therapist. I teach children to speak clearly and nicely, so that all the sounds come out right. In the morning I lay pictures out on the table and put up a mirror: in it you can see how your tongue moves. We do exercises for the tongue and lips, blow on a bit of cotton wool and play with words. My helpers are a mirror, pictures and a balloon. Many children only get the R sound at five or six years old. At school, English, music and reading aloud helped me most. And patience helped me a lot too! When a child manages a hard sound, we celebrate together.
a: To see how the tongue moves
To make light flash on the wall

job-socrabotnik.s: Hi! My name is David and I'm a social worker. I help older people who find it hard to manage things on their own. In the morning I pick up my bag and go to people's homes. I bring shopping from the shop and medicine from the pharmacy, and I help with cleaning. Often we just drink tea and chat, and I listen to stories about how people lived long ago. My helpers are a bag on wheels, a to-do list and a phone. At school, maths, English and good manners helped me most. In Russia there is even a Social Worker Day, on 8 June. I like that people wait for me and smile at the door.

job-policeiski.s: Hi! My name is Katie and I'm a police officer. My job is to help people and make sure everyone is safe. In the morning I check my radio and put on my uniform. Then I stand by the school and help children cross the road when the light is green. If a child is lost, I sit down beside them, ask their name and ring their parents, so they aren't scared. That's why it's good to know your own name and your mum's phone number. At school, PE and science helped me most. Jackets and rucksacks have reflective strips: in the dark they shine in the light of car headlamps, and a driver can see a person on foot from far away.
a: So people on foot can be seen in the dark

job-stroitel.s: Hi! My name is Ben and I'm a builder. In the morning I put on my hard hat and go to the building site. First we look at the plan: where the wall will be and where the window will go. Then I lay bricks next to my workmates, and high above us a crane is working. I need a spirit level, a trowel and a tape measure. A spirit level is a ruler with a bubble: if the bubble is in the middle, the wall stands straight. At school, maths and design and technology helped me. The happiest moment is when the house is finished and the windows light up. I think, “I built this!”

job-arhitektor.s: Hello! My name is Isabel and I'm an architect. I dream up houses, schools and bridges before anyone starts building them. In the morning I draw with a pencil, then I copy my drawing onto the computer. I also glue together a little model from cardboard, like a toy town. I need a pencil, a ruler and paper for plans. Art, maths and geography helped me most. The word “architect” comes from Greek and means “chief builder”. I feel happy walking down the street and seeing a house that I once drew.

job-elektrik.s: Hi! My name is Natalie and I'm an electrician. In the morning I drive to people whose light won't come on or whose socket doesn't work. First I switch off the power, and only then do I touch the wires. Wires come in different colours, so I don't mix them up. My helpers are a screwdriver, pliers and a gadget that shows whether there is electricity. The wires inside are made of copper: it carries electricity well. At school, science and maths helped me. The nicest moment is when I flick the switch and the room becomes bright.

job-santehnik.s: Hi! My name is Sam and I'm a plumber. I'm friends with water: I make sure it runs from the taps and doesn't drip from the pipes. In the morning I go out on calls, for example when a tap is leaking. In my bag I have an adjustable spanner, pipes and rubber washers. An adjustable spanner can change its size to fit any nut. At school, maths and science helped me. It's interesting that in a big building a pump lifts the water to the top floors. When the water runs in a smooth stream again, the people smile, and I like that very much.

job-avtomehanik.s: Hi! My name is Alice and I'm a car mechanic. I heal cars, like a doctor heals people. In the morning a car arrives that is making a strange noise. I lift it up on a ramp and listen for where something is knocking. I need a set of spanners, a jack and a gadget that reads messages from the car's computer. At school, science and maths helped me. One car has thousands of parts, and each one has its own job. In the evening the owner starts the engine, it purrs softly, and I feel glad: the car is well again.

job-tehnik-vetryak.s: Hi! My name is Thomas and I'm a wind turbine technician. A wind turbine is a huge tower with three blades that makes electricity from wind. In the morning I check the weather: when the wind is strong, nobody can work up high. Then I go up in a lift inside the tower, and at the very top I see fields and forests like in a picture. I always have a safety harness, a hard hat and a bag of tools with me. At school, science and geography helped me. A blade can be more than fifty metres long, and the turbine turns to face the wind all by itself.

job-montazhnik-solnechnyh.s: Hello! My name is Zoe and I'm a solar panel installer. I put panels on roofs that turn sunlight into electricity. In the morning my team and I take the panels to the house. I fix them to the roof and then join them up with wires. I need a cordless screwdriver, a tape measure and wires with special plugs. At school, science and maths helped me most. The panels work on a cloudy day too, just not as well as on a bright one. It's lovely when the family switch on the kettle and know that the sun made their tea.

job-inzhener-3d.s: Hello! My name is Max and I'm a 3D printing engineer. My printer doesn't print on paper, it prints objects: it lays down a thin string of plastic, layer by layer. In the morning I draw a new part on the computer, like a cogwheel or a toy dragon. Then I start the printer and wait for the part to grow. I need a computer, a printer and a reel of plastic. At school, maths, technical drawing and design and technology helped me. Sometimes printing takes many hours. The best bit is taking out the finished thing that wasn't there in the morning.
a: With one press, all at once

job-inzhener-elektromobilej.s: Hello! My name is Emily and I'm an electric car engineer. My cars run on electricity and make almost no noise. In the morning I check how the battery works: how long it holds its charge and how fast it charges. Then I go to the tests and watch how the car drives on the road. I need a computer, a charging station and a measuring gadget. At school, science, maths and computing helped me. Here's a fun fact: when an electric car brakes, the motor charges the battery a little. I'm happy that cars like these look after the clean air.

job-inzhener-robototehnik.s: Hello! My name is Oliver and I'm a robotics engineer. I build robots and teach them to follow commands. In the morning I check a helper robot: it has sensors, a motor and a small computer. Sensors are its eyes and ears: it sees an obstacle and goes round it. Then I write a program, and the robot does what it needs to. I need a screwdriver, a soldering iron and a laptop. At school, maths, computing and design and technology helped me. The word "robot" comes from the Czech language and means "hard work". I feel happy when my robot finds its own way.

job-lyotchik.s: Hello! My name is Sophie and I'm a pilot of a passenger plane. Before a flight I check the plane, the weather and the route. Then my co-pilot and I sit in the cockpit, where there are lots of screens and buttons. We talk by radio to air traffic controllers, who sit on the ground and help planes to fly and land. The plane climbs above the clouds, and up there the sun is always shining. Passenger planes usually fly at about ten kilometres high. At school, maths, science, geography and English helped me most: in the sky, pilots from all over the world understand each other in English.

job-voditel-avtobusa.s: Hello! My name is Jack and I'm a bus driver. In the morning I go to the depot and check the bus: the headlights, brakes, mirrors and doors. Then I drive along my route and stop at every bus stop. I say hello to the passengers, and many of them know my face. My helpers are the steering wheel, the big mirrors and the timetable. A bus is long, so on a corner I pull a little away from the kerb: the back of the bus swings out sideways. At school, maths, geography and the Highway Code helped me most. I love it when children wave to me from the window.

job-mashinist.s: Hello! My name is Hannah and I'm a train driver. In the morning I go to the station and check the locomotive: the dials, lights, brakes and horn. Then I get my route and drive the train along the rails. On the way I watch the signals and talk to the controller by radio. Fields, bridges and towns flash past the window. My helpers are the control desk, the radio and the clock. At school, maths, science and paying attention helped me most. You know, a train takes a long time to stop, sometimes hundreds of metres, so I spot the signals early.
a: The train takes a long time to stop
The train can't hear the horn

job-kapitan-korablya.s: Hello! My name is Harry and I'm a ship's captain. In the morning I look at the chart and find out what the weather will be. Then I give the order and we leave the quay. I stand on the bridge, where you can see the sea well. My helpers are the compass, binoculars, the chart and the ship's wheel. A captain is responsible for the ship and for everyone on board. A ship's speed is measured in knots: one knot is one nautical mile an hour, which is 1852 metres. At school, geography, science and maths helped me most. I love the evening when the sun sets right into the water.

job-kosmonavt.s: Hello! My name is Tom and I'm an astronaut. Morning on the station begins with exercise: without it, muscles get weak in weightlessness. Then I watch the instruments, do experiments and take photos of the Earth through the window. My helpers are a spacesuit, exercise machines and a camera. Before my flight I studied and trained for several years. At school, science, maths and PE helped me most. And the station goes round the Earth in about an hour and a half, so in one day we see the sunrise sixteen times. We sleep in sleeping bags fastened to the wall.

job-operator-dronov.s: Hello! My name is Grace and I'm a drone operator. A drone is a small flying machine with propellers, and I control it with a remote. In the morning I check that it's charged and that the propellers are not broken. Today I'm filming a field from above for a farmer, and tomorrow I'll take medicine to a village across the river. Sometimes a drone helps to find a mushroom picker who got lost in the forest: it has a camera that can see heat. My tools are the remote, a tablet with a map and spare batteries. At school, geography, science and maths helped me. There is a strict rule: you must not fly a drone near an airport, because planes fly there.

job-povar.s: Hello! My name is George and I'm a chef. In the morning the kitchen smells of fresh bread and herbs. I put on a clean apron and a tall hat, wash my hands and start cooking. I need a sharp knife, a frying pan and scales to measure everything exactly by the recipe. I chop vegetables, make soup and taste it with a spoon. At school, maths and science helped me, because food changes when it is heated. Here's something interesting: a tomato is, scientifically, a berry. Most of all I'm happy when a guest says: "Thank you, that was delicious!"

job-pekar.s: Hello! My name is Molly and I'm a baker. I get up very early, while it is still dark outside. First I mix dough from flour, water and yeast. Yeast is made of tiny living fungi: they make bubbles, and the dough rises. Then I shape bread rolls and put them in the oven. I need bowls, scales and a peel for the oven. At school, maths and science helped me. When people come in the morning, the bread is still warm, and the bakery smells so good that everyone smiles.

job-portnoj.s: Hello! My name is Alice and I'm a tailor and a clothes designer. I think up dresses, jackets and suits and sew them myself. First I draw a sketch: what the thing will look like. Then I measure the person with a tape measure and make a pattern, a paper model of the pieces. I need scissors, a needle and a sewing machine. At school, art, maths and design and technology helped me. People had needles with an eye as far back as the Stone Age. When someone puts on something I made and feels happy, it makes me very glad.
a: A paper model of the pieces

job-balerina.s: Hello! My name is Lily and I'm a ballet dancer. My day begins with a class at the barre, where I warm up my legs and back. Then comes rehearsal: we repeat the dance many times until it feels light. In the evening I step onto the stage in a beautiful costume and dance to an orchestra. I dance in pointe shoes, which have a hard toe, and I sew on the ribbons myself. At school, music, PE and English helped me. Pointe shoes wear out quickly, so I need new ones. When the audience claps, I feel happy.

job-muzykant.s: Hello! My name is Daniel and I'm a musician and I play the cello. In the morning I play a few scales so my fingers wake up. Then I rehearse with my friends, and in the evening I give a concert. I need a cello, a bow and sheet music. A cello has four strings, and the bow is strung with hair from a horse's tail. At school, music, maths and English helped me. A cello is big, so I play sitting down and hold it between my knees. When the hall goes quiet and listens, I feel that music brings everyone together.

job-dirizher.s: Hello! My name is Charlotte and I'm a conductor. I stand in front of an orchestra, where sometimes a whole hundred musicians play. I don't play myself, but with my hands I show when to come in and how to play: quietly or loudly, fast or slowly. In the morning I read the score, big sheet music where the parts of all the instruments are written together. I need a baton, a music stand and the score. At school, music and maths helped me. When the orchestra sounds like one, I feel very happy.

job-akter.s: Hello! My name is Oliver and I'm an actor. I work in a theatre, and I turn into a captain one day and a kind wizard the next. In the daytime we have rehearsals, where we learn our parts and work out how to move and speak. Before the play I put on my costume, and the make-up artist draws a moustache or wrinkles on my face. I need a part to play, a costume and make-up. At school, English, music and PE helped me. In Russian theatres, three bells ring before a play begins. When the audience laughs or feels sad along with me, I know I did a good job.

job-animator.s: Hello! My name is Emily and I'm an animator, which means I make cartoons. I draw a character many times, and in every drawing it moves just a tiny bit. When the drawings change quickly, the character comes alive and walks, jumps or laughs. In the morning I think up the movement, then I draw on a graphics tablet. I need a tablet, a pencil and a computer. At school, art, English and maths helped me. Just one second of a cartoon needs twelve or even twenty-four drawings. I love it when my character smiles out of the screen.
a: Takes a photo of a face

job-fotograf.s: Hello! My name is Harry and I'm a photographer. I catch lovely moments: a laugh, a sunset, a first step. In the morning I choose where to take pictures, so the light is soft. Then I go to the park, look through the camera and press the button. I need a camera, a lens, a tripod and a flash. A tripod has three legs, so the photo doesn't wobble. At school, art, science and geography helped me. The word “photograph” comes from Greek and means “drawing with light”. The best part is when people look at a picture and say, “How lovely it came out!”

job-videomontazhyor.s: Hello! My name is Grace and I'm a video editor. I put a film together from little pieces that were filmed with a camera. Films are not shot in order, so I arrange the scenes to make a story. I pick the best shots, choose music and add words on the screen. I need a computer, editing software and headphones. At school, English, music and computing helped me. It's funny that many hours of filming become a film that's only an hour or two long. I'm happy when the audience watches a film and forgets it was put together from little pieces.
a: Puts a film together from little pieces

job-zvukorezhisser.s: Hello! My name is Jack and I'm a sound engineer. I make sure everything can be heard well: voices, music and noises. In the morning I set up the microphones and check that the wires aren't buzzing. Then I sit at a big mixing desk and move the sliders: this voice louder, that one quieter. I need a microphone, a mixing desk and headphones. At school, music, science and maths helped me. In films, footsteps and creaking doors are often recorded separately. And the crunch of snow can be made by squeezing cornflour in a bag. I love it when the audience hears everything as if they were inside the story.

job-uchitel-nachalnyh-klassov.s: Hello! My name is Hannah and I'm a primary school teacher. In the morning I get to school before anyone else and lay out the exercise books, chalk and colourful cards. Then the bell rings and my little Year 1 children run into the classroom. We learn to read, count, write and draw. My best helpers are the board, the pointer and picture books. I've used every subject at once, especially English, maths and singing. The happiest moment is when a child reads a word all by themselves for the first time and is amazed: “I can do it!” I'm always learning too, often from the children.

job-bibliotekar.s: Hello! My name is George and I'm a librarian. In the morning I open the doors, switch on the lights and put the books that were returned yesterday back on the shelves. On the spine of every book there is a code, like the address of a house: it shows where the book belongs. Then the readers come, and I help them find a book about dinosaurs, about the sea, or a funny story. My helpers are the catalogue, the book trolley and the computer. At school, reading, English and literature helped me. The nicest part is reading aloud to little ones: they listen without a sound.

job-hranitel-muzeya.s: Hello! My name is Olivia and I'm a museum curator. I look after old things: paintings, dishes, coins and toys. In the morning I check the temperature and the damp in the rooms: old things need steady air, like a warm coat for us in freezing weather. Then I look at an object through a magnifying glass and write in a log book how it is feeling. My tools are a magnifying glass, gloves and a log book. At school, history, art and maths helped me. And only some of the treasures are on show: the rest wait quietly in special storerooms, and they come out into the galleries in turns.

job-zhurnalist.s: Hello! My name is Ben and I'm a journalist. In the morning I find out where to go: for example, to the opening of a new zoo. I take a notebook, a voice recorder and a camera. I ask people questions, listen carefully and write down the answers. Then I sit down to write an article and think up a headline that makes people want to read it. The main rule is to check that every word is true. At school, English, reading and science helped me. Sometimes a short piece is harder to write than a long one: it's hard to say things briefly.

job-perevodchik.s: Hello! My name is Sophie and I'm a translator. I help people who speak different languages understand each other. In the morning I open a book and a dictionary and translate page after page. Sometimes I work at meetings: I listen through headphones and tell the others what was said almost straight away. My tools are a dictionary, headphones and books. At school, English, modern languages and reading helped me. You can't translate word for word: in Russia a cockerel crows “ku-ka-re-ku”, while in English it says “cock-a-doodle-doo”, and in other countries people hear completely different words.

job-sudya.s: Hello! My name is Oliver and I am a judge. Sometimes two people argue and cannot agree by themselves, for example two neighbours who cannot agree about a fence. They come to court. I put on a black robe and listen to both sides without interrupting. Then I read the papers and the law. The law is a set of rules that are the same for everyone. I decide fairly, without helping anyone or hurting anyone. My tools are the law, my robe and my papers. At school, history, citizenship and English helped me. Statues of Themis, the goddess of justice, hold a pair of scales. They remind us to weigh the words of both sides.

job-arheolog.s: Hello! My name is Tom and I'm an archaeologist. In summer we go on a dig, put up tents and carefully remove the soil layer by layer. We don't work with a big spade, but with a little trowel and a brush, so we don't damage what we find. We wash, draw and measure every broken bit of pot and write down where we found it. At school, history, maths and art helped me. And did you know, in Veliky Novgorod in Russia, letters written on birch bark were found: they were written with a sharp stick. Among them are drawings by a boy called Onfim, who drew little people on bark a very long time ago.

job-geolog.s: Hello! My name is Ella and I'm a geologist. In the morning we go on a hike to the cliffs or a ravine, because rocks tell you most about themselves right where they are. I take a geological hammer, a compass and a magnifying glass. I chip off a small piece, look at it through the magnifying glass and write down where I found it. Rocks are tested for hardness: the softest mineral, talc, can be scratched with a fingernail, and the hardest is diamond. In the evening by the campfire I draw a map. At school, geography, chemistry and art helped me.

job-astronom.s: Hello! My name is Leo and I'm an astronomer. Most of my work is at night: when it gets dark, I go to the observatory and open the dome. The telescope turns towards the stars, and the camera takes pictures of them. In the daytime I sleep a little, and then I go through the pictures on the computer. My tools are a telescope, a camera and a computer. At school, science, maths and geography helped me. Sunlight takes a little more than eight minutes to reach us, while the light of faraway stars travels for many years, so we see them as they were long ago.

job-meteorolog.s: Hello! My name is Amelia and I'm a meteorologist, and people also call me a weather forecaster. In the morning I look at maps from satellites and at the instruments of the weather station: how many degrees it is, which way the wind blows, where it's raining. From them I tell people what the weather will be tomorrow. Twice a day, weather stations send up a balloon with a light instrument, called a radiosonde. It rises higher than aeroplanes and reports how cold and damp it is up there. At school, geography, science and maths helped me. And snowflakes almost always have six sides, and I love looking at them in winter.

job-klimatolog.s: Hello! My name is Sam and I'm a climate scientist. Weather is what's outside the window today, and climate is the weather we usually get in our part of the world over many years. It is usually counted over thirty years. In the morning I go through tables of temperatures and rainfall and draw graphs. Sometimes I look at a slice of an old tree trunk: in warm, wet years the yearly ring is wider, so a tree keeps a memory of the past. My tools are a computer, a thermometer and a magnifying glass. At school, geography, maths and science helped me.

job-morskoy-biolog.s: Hello! My name is Lily and I'm a marine biologist. Early in the morning we go out to sea in a boat, and then I dive in with a mask and flippers. Under the water I look at fish, crabs and seaweed, take pictures of them with an underwater camera and write in a special notebook with plastic pages, because paper would go soggy in the water. My tools are a mask, an underwater camera and a notebook like that. At school, biology, geography and maths helped me. And an octopus has three hearts, and its blood is blue.

job-sci-fizik-uskoritel.s: Hello! My name is Hannah, I'm a physicist and I work at a big particle accelerator, called a collider. It is a huge ring, twenty-seven kilometres around, hidden deep underground. Tiny particles race round it at almost the speed of light, then crash into each other, and we look at what happened. Our big question: what is the world made of at the very, very smallest level? Sometimes a "signal" shows up in the data, and then it turns out to be just interference, so we honestly cross it out. We work in a big team from many countries and check each other's work: in 2012 two separate groups found signs of the same particle, the Higgs boson. My tools are powerful magnets, detectors and computers. At school, physics, maths and a foreign language helped me. And the magnets in the ring are cooled to almost minus two hundred and seventy degrees, which is colder than space.

job-sci-genetik.s: Hello! My name is Daniel, I'm a geneticist. In every living cell there is DNA, a long set of instructions for building the body. It is written with just four "letters", and from it come flies, birch trees and people. I study fruit flies: I want to find out which part of the instructions is in charge of the colour of their eyes. One day we noticed that the same "letter" affects two features at once. At first I thought I had made a mistake and asked my colleagues to repeat the experiment, and they got the same result. My tools are a microscope, test tubes and a computer that compares long records. At school, biology, maths and English helped me, because I read the "text" of life. And the DNA of any two people is the same in almost ninety-nine point nine per cent.

job-sci-himik-materialy.s: Hello! My name is Emily, I'm a chemist, and I invent new materials. My question: how can we make something very light but strong? I mix different substances in glass containers, heat them, cool them and see what comes out. One of my favourite materials is aerogel, which is called "frozen smoke". My first samples cracked and crumbled, and only after many tries did I understand that they must be dried very slowly. We write down our work so exactly that a colleague can repeat it and check it. My tools are scales, test tubes and a microscope. At school, chemistry, maths and physics helped me. And do you know, aerogel is almost all air, but it can hold up many times its own weight.

job-sci-neurobiolog.s: Hello! My name is Jack, I'm a neuroscientist: I study how the brain works. It has about eighty-six billion neurons, which are tiny cells that send signals to each other. My question: what happens in the brain when we remember something? We watch mice in a maze and see how they find their way, and how they get faster each time. One day, mice that had slept well remembered the path better than those that hadn't slept. We didn't believe ourselves straight away and repeated the experiment many times with different groups. Now we think that during sleep the brain sorts new knowledge into its places. My tools are a microscope, a computer and a maze. At school, biology, maths and English helped me. And the brain weighs just over a kilogram, but uses about a fifth of all the body's energy.

job-sci-matematik.s: Hello! My name is Grace, I'm a mathematician. My main question: can we prove that something is true always, and not only in examples? I work with a pencil, paper and a computer. In the city of Königsberg there were seven bridges, and people argued about whether you could cross each one exactly once. Many tried, and in 1736 Leonhard Euler proved that you can't, without ever having to walk over a single bridge. I make mistakes too: I write a proof, a colleague finds a hole in it, and together we mend it. That's how it should be: a proof must stand up to any check. At school, maths, logic and drawing helped me. And there are infinitely many prime numbers, which divide only by one and by themselves. People knew this more than two thousand years ago.

job-sci-vrach-vakciny.s: Hello! My name is Thomas, I'm a medical researcher: I help to create medicines and vaccines. A vaccine teaches the body to recognise a disease in advance, so that it can deal with it quickly later. First we study the new medicine in the laboratory, under a microscope. Sometimes it doesn't work, and then we start all over again, and that is a result too. If the medicine looks good, it is carefully tested with volunteers, and doctors and independent experts watch every step. For me it is important that everything is honest and not rushed. My tools are a microscope, test tubes and a computer. At school, biology, chemistry and maths helped me. The word "vaccine" comes from the Latin word "vacca", which means "cow": the first vaccine was invented more than two hundred years ago, and it used cowpox.

job-sci-vulkanolog.s: Hello! My name is Sophie, I'm a volcanologist. My job is to understand what a volcano is doing and when it might wake up. In summer we go to Kamchatka in Russia, where there are many volcanoes, and watch them from a safe distance. We set up instruments that can hear quiet tremors underground, and we also film the slopes with a thermal camera, a camera that sees heat. One day an instrument showed strange tremors, and then it turned out that a rockfall had just come down, so we decided to always compare the readings of different instruments. We talk over the results with colleagues from all over the country. My tools are a seismograph, a thermal camera and a computer. At school, geography, physics and chemistry helped me. And Klyuchevskaya Sopka in Kamchatka is the highest active volcano in Eurasia, more than four and a half kilometres high.

job-sci-astrofizik-teleskop.s: Hello! My name is Ben, I'm an astrophysicist and I work with a space telescope. It flies very far from Earth, about one and a half million kilometres away, and we control it from here. Its main mirror is six and a half metres wide and is put together from eighteen hexagonal pieces. The telescope sees infrared light, which our eyes can't notice, so it looks right through clouds of space dust. My question: how are stars and the very first galaxies born? Sometimes a picture comes out with interference, and we check it one after another in different ways. If we find something unusual, we wait until other groups confirm it. My tools are a telescope, a computer and a program for processing pictures. At school, physics, maths and computing helped me. And the mirrors are covered with a thin layer of gold, because it reflects infrared light well.

job-fermer.s: Hello! My name is George and I am a farmer. My day starts early, before the sun comes up. First I feed the cows and hens, then I collect the eggs and milk the cows. In the daytime I drive my tractor to cut grass for hay or to sow oats. In the evening I mend the fence and check that all the animals are home. My helpers are the tractor, the buckets and the pitchfork. At school, science, maths and design and technology helped me most. Did you know that a cow's stomach has four parts, and she chews her food twice? But what I love most is early morning, when mist lies over the field.

job-smotritel-zooparka.s: Hello! My name is Harry and I am a zookeeper. I look after the animals: I feed them, clean up and make sure they are happy. In the morning I go to the giraffes with a bucket of leaves and twigs. Then I wash their enclosure and check that everyone is well and cheerful. For my work I need a bucket, a broom and a trolley of food. You have to know each animal's habits: what it likes to eat and when it sleeps. At school, science and geography helped me most. Did you know that a giraffe's tongue is about 45 centimetres long and dark in colour? I am happy when children are amazed and ask lots of questions.

job-sadovnik.s: Hello! My name is Emily and I am a gardener and landscape designer. I think up ways to make a yard, a park or a garden beautiful. First I draw a plan on paper: where the path will go, where the bench will be and where the flower bed will be. Then my team and I dig the earth and plant trees, bushes and flowers. My helpers are a spade, secateurs, which are special scissors for branches, and a measuring tape. At school, art, maths and science helped me most. Did you know that you can see rings on a cut tree trunk? As many rings as there are, that is how many years the tree grew. In spring I am happy when the tulips I planted come out.

job-pererabotka-musora.s: Hello! My name is Jack and I work at a plant where rubbish is recycled. We give things a second life. In the morning lorries arrive with paper, plastic, glass and metal cans. All of it travels along a long belt, and we and clever machines sort the waste into kinds. A magnet pulls out the iron, and other machines pick out the plastic and paper. Then everything goes off to be made into something new. At school, science, geography and maths helped me most. Glass can be melted down again and again, and it does not get worse. I like it that children in schools collect old paper.

job-lesnik.s: Hello! My name is Sophie and I am a forest ranger. I look after the forest so that it stays healthy and beautiful. In the morning I go on my rounds with a rucksack, a compass and binoculars. I check that the trees are not ill, that there is no litter and that nobody has left a fire burning. In spring we plant little saplings of firs and pines. If I meet an elk, a hare or a fox on the way, I am happy and write it in my notebook. At school, science, geography and orienteering helped me most. Did you know that forest ants are the cleaners of the forest? They eat lots of harmful insects. That is why anthills must never be broken.

job-programmist.s: Hello! My name is Thomas and I am a computer programmer. I write instructions for the computer, called programs, so that it knows what to do. In the morning I drink my tea and look for what is broken: a mistake in a program is called a “bug”. A computer understands everything very exactly: if you write it wrong, it does it wrong. My tools are a keyboard, a code editor and a programming language. At school, maths, English and logic helped me. The world's first program for a calculating machine was thought up by a woman called Ada, more than 150 years ago.

job-razrabotchik-prilozheniy.s: Hello! My name is Grace and I am an app developer. An app is a program for a phone or a tablet, for example a game or a picture book. In the morning my team and I decide what to make better in it. Then I write the program and test it on small and big screens, on old and new phones. My tools are a computer, a phone for testing and paper sketches. Many apps are first drawn on paper with a pencil. At school, maths, computing and art helped me. The nicest part is when a child uses the app and smiles.

job-geymdizayner.s: Hello! My name is Leo and I am a game designer. I think up games: the rules, the heroes and the levels. In the morning I draw a map of a new level on a sheet of paper. Then I let my friends play, and I watch where they get bored and where it is too hard. A game is changed many times until it becomes fun. My tools are cards, paper and a computer. At school, maths, art and English literature helped me. The game with falling shapes that people know all over the world was invented in Moscow in 1984.

job-dizayner-interfeysov.s: Hello! My name is Hannah and I am an interface designer. That means I make apps and websites easy to use. An interface is what you see and press: buttons, pictures, menus. I invite a person, ask them to try the app and quietly watch where they get muddled. If they get muddled, the mistake is mine, not theirs. My tools are a pencil, a tablet and a program for drawing screens. At school, art, maths and English helped me. Some doors make you want to push, but you have to pull, and a good interface should never be like that.
a: The person who made the app

job-specialist-po-dannym.s: Hello! My name is Daniel and I am a data specialist. Data is lots of numbers and facts in tables. I collect them, check them, count them and draw graphs from them. For example, I find out at what times the bus is fullest and when to send another one. My tools are a table, a computer and a graph. At school, maths, computing and English helped me. A picture often says more than a hundred lines: on a graph the eye sees at once where the numbers are bigger and where they are smaller. The nicest part is when my graph helps make something easier for people.

job-kiberbezopasnost.s: Hello! My name is Charlotte and I am a cyber security specialist. I guard computers and data from tricksters, like a watchman guards a house. In the morning I check for updates: they close the holes in programs. Then I explain simple rules to my colleagues: do not open strange links and never tell anyone your password. My tools are a protection program, a password manager and updates. At school, maths, computing and logic helped me. And a long password made of several words is stronger than a short one with symbols. It is easier to remember and harder to guess.
a: A long one, made of several words
One made of just a name

job-trener-po-kibersportu.s: Hello! My name is William and I am an esports coach. My team competes in computer games. Our morning starts with exercise and warming up our hands. Then we play and talk about what went well and what did not, and we learn to work things out together. Our main rules are breaks, walks and healthy sleep. Once every twenty minutes you should look into the distance for twenty seconds, which protects your eyes. My tools are a computer, a stopwatch and a notebook for review. At school, maths, PE and English helped me.

job-bloger.s: Hello! My name is Olivia and I am a blogger. I make videos about how the world works: why it rains and how a bean plant grows. I work a few hours a day, and the rest of the time I go for walks, meet friends and do sport. First I think up a topic and read books, and then I check all the facts. Then I film and edit. I delete rude comments, answer the kind ones and do not chase likes. My tools are a camera, a microphone and an editing program. At school, English, science and art helped me.

job-ai-researcher.s: Hello! My name is Emily and I research artificial intelligence. That means I work out how to teach a computer program to do something new. In the morning I read what other scientists have found, and then I try my idea on the computer. The program looks for patterns in a huge number of examples. It counts very fast and never gets tired. But only people can decide what is worth studying and what is good for people. I also notice when the program makes a mistake, and I look for why it happened. At school I used maths, computing and English, because I have to explain my discoveries clearly. Fun fact: the words “artificial intelligence” were made up about seventy years ago, before there were computers at home.

job-ai-ml-engineer.s: Hello! My name is Oliver and I am a machine learning engineer. I teach a program with examples. I show it thousands of photos of cats and dogs, and it looks for how they are different. The program looks very fast and never gets tired, so it can go through more pictures than a person could see in a whole life. Then I test it on new photos and write down where it gets things wrong. I think about which examples it was missing, and I add them. A person has to decide what to teach it and which answer counts as good. At school I used maths and computing, and also patience. Fun fact: in one experiment, a program told wolves from dogs by the snow around them, not by the animal. That is why it always gets checked.
a: He turns the computer off for ever

job-ai-robot-engineer.s: Hello! My name is Harry and I am a robotics engineer. My robot with a mechanical arm is learning to pick things up: an apple, a cup, a cube. First I build the arm and connect a camera, and then the program tries again and again. It remembers what worked, and each time it grabs a little better. The robot never gets bored or lazy, and it can try thousands of times. But it sometimes squeezes a soft apple too hard, and then I work out what went wrong and fix it all. Only people can decide why a robot needs an arm and how it will help people. At school I used science, maths and design and technology. Fun fact: robots often practise first in a computer game, where they can try many times and nothing breaks.

job-ai-radiologist.s: Hello! My name is Charlotte and I am a radiologist, a doctor who looks at scans. In the morning the pictures come to me: lungs, little bones, sometimes a head. I look at them on a big screen and write a report for the doctor who is looking after the patient. A program with artificial intelligence helps me. It has seen a great many pictures and points out where something may look unusual. It works fast and never gets tired, but it sometimes makes mistakes, for example it takes a shadow for a problem. That is why I decide: I look myself, I think about the person, and I tell the doctor what I see. At school I used biology, physics and careful looking. Fun fact: X-rays were found in 1895 by the scientist Wilhelm Röntgen, and in some countries they are named after him.

job-ai-safety.s: Hello! My name is Amelia and I am a specialist in the safety and ethics of artificial intelligence. I check that a clever program is honest and kind. Every morning I ask it tricky questions and see what it answers. If the program upsets someone, or gives a made-up thing as the truth, I write it down, and my team and I put it right. A computer finds patterns quickly, but it does not really understand what being polite or fair means. People decide that. At school I used English, science and computing. Fun fact: a program sometimes writes untrue things in a very sure voice, so important facts should always be checked in books and with grown-ups.
a: Writes it down and puts it right

job-ai-designer.s: Hello! My name is George and I am a designer of products with artificial intelligence. I work out how people can use a clever helper easily and clearly. In the morning I draw screens and buttons, and then I watch how different people get on with them: grannies and schoolchildren too. I also write instructions for the helper, called prompts: answer politely, keep it simple and do not make things up. The program reads them at once and never gets tired, but it does not know what people need. I do, because I listen to them. If the helper answers in a strange way, I notice and rewrite the prompt. At school I used art, English and computing. Fun fact: the same request, said in different ways, can be understood very differently by a program.

job-ai-agronomist-drones.s: Hello! My name is Jack and I am a crop specialist, and drones and sensors work in my field. In the morning a drone with a camera flies over the rows and photographs every plant. Sensors in the soil tell me if it is dry or damp. A program with artificial intelligence compares thousands of photos and says: here the leaves look poorly. It sees the whole field at once and never gets tired. But I am the one who walks to that spot: I touch the leaves, look at the soil and decide how to help the plant. Sometimes the program makes a mistake and takes a shadow for a disease. At school I used biology, geography and maths. Fun fact: a drone's camera can see light that our eyes cannot, and with it healthy leaves look different from weak ones.

job-ai-translator-editor.s: Hello! My name is Sophie and I am a translator and editor. First a program does a machine translation: in a minute it has a whole page ready. Then I read it and correct it. The program is fast, never gets tired, and knows which words usually stand next to each other. But sometimes it does not get a joke, or mixes up a word with two meanings, like “bat” for the animal and “bat” for cricket. People feel what the author meant to say, and choose warm, lovely words. That matters most in children's books. At school I used English, a foreign language and literature. Fun fact: there are about seven thousand languages on Earth, and people are still teaching programs to understand them.

job-ai-forecaster.s: Hello! My name is Thomas and I am a weather forecaster. I study weather and climate. In the morning I look at what satellites, radars and instruments on balloons show. All these numbers are collected into a huge table. A program with artificial intelligence finds patterns in it that are like ones from the past, and quickly works out what comes next. It never gets tired and can check many possibilities. But weather is tricky, and a forecast can be wrong. I compare the answers and decide what to tell people, for example: take an umbrella. At school I used geography, maths and science. Fun fact: every day, all over the world, balloons with instruments are sent up, and they measure the air high above the ground.
a: They measure the air high up

job-uchitel-ii.s: Hello! My name is Samuel and I am an artificial intelligence teacher. I teach a computer program, for example to recognise animals in photos. I do not teach with lessons but with examples: I show thousands of pictures of cats and dogs and say which is which. Then I check the answers: sometimes the program gets it wrong, for example it takes a fluffy hat for a cat. I correct it and show more. My tools are a computer, folders of examples and a checking table. At school, maths, computing and English helped me. The program does not understand a cat as you do: it looks in pictures for what repeats often.

job-own-bakery.s: Hello! My name is Ana, and I have my own bakery in a small town in the north of Portugal. The shop in our street had closed, and there was no fresh bread in the mornings. At first I baked at home and gave rolls to the neighbours. My first loaves came out as hard as stones, so I baked again until they were soft. Now I have two helpers, and we get up at four in the morning. The flour, butter and eggs for one roll cost $2, and I sell it for $3. That leaves $1, and I use it to pay for the rent, the electricity and my helpers, and I save up for a new oven. My customers are neighbours on their way to work and parents after school. At school, maths helped me to count grams and dollars, and so did biology: yeast is a tiny living fungus that makes dough fluffy. I used to work in somebody else's bakery, and I liked it there too.
